set.stem: A 49-year-old man returns from a holiday in Portugal, where he stayed in a hotel and was in contact with a nephew who had influenza. He has fever, dry cough, breathlessness and confusion; his wife reports that at one point he did not recognise her. The chest X-ray shows bilateral infiltrates. What is the most useful diagnostic test?
set.explanation: The differential includes Legionella (hotel water systems, confusion) and influenza (a sick contact), and a multiplex nucleic acid amplification (PCR) test on sputum or a nasopharyngeal swab detects Legionella, influenza, Mycoplasma and other respiratory pathogens rapidly enough to guide treatment and infection control; Legionella urinary antigen is a useful addition. Paired serology gives only a retrospective answer 2–4 weeks later, HRCT and lavage cell counts do not identify an organism, and sputum cytology looks for malignant cells.

set.stem: A 53-year-old man has had a non-productive cough for 3 months. His spirometry is normal and he already takes omeprazole for reflux. Which statement about his management is true?
set.explanation: Chronic cough (more than 8 weeks) should be assessed with a chest X-ray and spirometry in every patient, to exclude lung cancer, tuberculosis, bronchiectasis and interstitial disease before treating the common causes (asthma or eosinophilic bronchitis, rhinosinusitis, reflux). An inhaled corticosteroid trial is reasonable only once serious disease is excluded and ideally when FeNO or eosinophils suggest type 2 inflammation, ENT referral is not first line, dismissing it as habit is inappropriate, and increasing the acid suppressant helps only when reflux is proved to be the cause.

set.stem: A 35-year-old woman with asthma attends clinic with deteriorating control. For 48 hours she has had fever of 38.6°C, a cough productive of green sputum and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. Her CRP is 180 mg/L with a neutrophilia; blood eosinophils are normal. Her chest X-ray is shown. What is the most likely cause of the deterioration?
set.explanation: An acute 48-hour febrile illness with purulent sputum, pleuritic pain, a high CRP with neutrophilia and right lower-zone consolidation is bacterial pneumonia, which has triggered the asthma exacerbation and needs antibiotics (amoxicillin for low severity) alongside the asthma treatment. Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis also occurs in asthmatics but produces recurrent fleeting infiltrates, brown mucus plugs, blood eosinophilia and a very high IgE; viral infections are the commonest trigger of asthma attacks but do not produce focal consolidation with a CRP this high, and mycobacterial and parasitic infections have a slower course.

why: Source key (fungal infection/ABPA) was not supported by a 48-hour pleuritic illness with focal consolidation; discriminating data added and key changed to bacterial infection

set.explanation: A short history of fever, pleuritic pain and rusty sputum is classic pneumococcal lobar pneumonia, and cold sores are common because the febrile illness reactivates latent herpes simplex virus. HSV itself very rarely causes pneumonia except in immunosuppressed or ventilated patients. Aspergillus, Pneumocystis and M. tuberculosis cause subacute illness in susceptible hosts rather than an acute lobar pneumonia in a healthy man.

Fever and pneumonia within 14 days of travel to the Arabian Peninsula meet the case definition for possible Middle East respiratory syndrome (MERS coronavirus, spread from camels and within hospitals), so the patient must be isolated with airborne precautions and have respiratory samples sent for MERS-CoV PCR while standard CAP treatment is started. Melioidosis (Burkholderia pseudomallei) is a South-East Asian and northern Australian infection, SARS has not circulated since 2004, and CPE screening concerns carriage of resistant Gram-negatives rather than the cause of pneumonia.

Pneumonia developing 48 hours or more after admission is hospital-acquired and is caused more often by Gram-negative bacilli (Enterobacteriaceae, Pseudomonas) and Staphylococcus aureus including MRSA, so antibiotics follow the local HAP policy, which is based on local resistance patterns and time since admission. The CAP protocol would give inadequate cover, ventilator-associated pneumonia applies only to intubated patients, and waiting for cultures in a confused patient with a new infiltrate is unsafe. A CTPA is considered if the picture suggests pulmonary embolism, but a new infiltrate with acute confusion points to infection or aspiration.

set.stem: A 72-year-old man admitted 8 days ago with an exacerbation of COPD was initially improving but now spikes a fever, with green blood-streaked sputum and dense left-sided consolidation on the chest X-ray. Late-onset hospital-acquired pneumonia is most often caused by which of the following?
set.explanation: Late-onset HAP (5 or more days after admission) is caused mainly by resistant Gram-negative bacilli such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Klebsiella and other Enterobacteriaceae and Acinetobacter baumannii, plus MRSA, so broad-spectrum antibiotics guided by local policy are needed. Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae are typical of community-acquired and early-onset HAP, while Chlamydia and Legionella are community-acquired atypical organisms.

Hospital-acquired pneumonia is the second commonest hospital-acquired infection and carries a mortality of around 30%, much higher than community-acquired pneumonia, because patients are older and sicker and the organisms are more resistant; ventilator-associated pneumonia is worse still. Prevention includes head-up positioning, oral hygiene, early mobilisation and minimising sedation and aspiration risk.

In an injecting drug user with a groin injection-site abscess, high fever and multiple peripheral nodules that cavitate, the explanation is right-sided (tricuspid) endocarditis, usually Staphylococcus aureus, shedding septic emboli to the lungs. Blood cultures and echocardiography are the key tests. Aspiration gives dependent consolidation or a single abscess, metastases rarely cavitate and do not cause high fever, bland thromboemboli do not produce multiple cavitating nodules, and tuberculosis is more indolent.

set.stem: A 54-year-old man is due to start anti-TNF monoclonal antibody therapy for Crohn's disease. He had BCG vaccination in childhood and his chest X-ray shows a minor abnormality. Which statement about the interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) is true?
set.explanation: IGRAs measure interferon-gamma released by T cells stimulated with M. tuberculosis-specific antigens (ESAT-6, CFP-10) that are absent from BCG and most environmental mycobacteria, so they are more specific than the tuberculin skin test in BCG-vaccinated people. A positive IGRA shows sensitisation, not active disease: before anti-TNF therapy it prompts exclusion of active tuberculosis and then treatment of latent infection (e.g. 3 months of rifampicin plus isoniazid), not full antituberculous chemotherapy. It is not a test for active TB and it measures interferon-gamma, not alpha.

set.stem: A 64-year-old woman with back pain and weight loss has a fluctuant, fluid-filled flank mass, from which pus is aspirated. What is the most important additional test on the pus?
set.explanation: A 'cold' flank or psoas abscess with back pain and weight loss is typical of spinal tuberculosis (Pott disease) tracking along the psoas sheath, so the pus must be sent for AFB smear, mycobacterial culture and rapid molecular testing; MRI of the spine then shows the vertebral and disc involvement. Routine fluid biochemistry and flow cytometry would not identify the cause, bronchoscopy is not indicated without pulmonary disease, and an echocardiogram is for suspected endocarditis rather than a single cold abscess.

set.stem: A 28-year-old woman develops painful red nodules on both shins, ankle arthralgia and fever, and her chest X-ray (shown) is performed. At 4-week review she feels well apart from mild lethargy. What is the most likely cause?
set.explanation: The film shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy; with erythema nodosum, ankle arthritis and fever in a young woman this is Löfgren syndrome, an acute form of sarcoidosis that usually resolves spontaneously within 1–2 years and is managed with NSAIDs and observation. Lymphoma and tuberculosis can cause hilar nodes, but tuberculous nodes are usually unilateral and lymphoma would not settle within weeks; HIV and pneumonia do not produce this triad.

Multiple smooth, well-defined nodules unchanged for 5 years in a woman with long-standing seropositive rheumatoid arthritis are rheumatoid (necrobiotic) nodules, which may cavitate and are associated with subcutaneous nodules; Caplan syndrome is the variant in coal or silica-exposed workers. Stability over 5 years excludes metastatic cancer, pulmonary fibrosis gives reticulation rather than discrete nodules, and neither bronchiectasis nor pulmonary embolism produces multiple smooth nodules.

set.stem: A 64-year-old man presents with high fever, left-sided pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness; his chest X-ray is shown. Pleural fluid is turbid with pH 7.0, glucose 1.1 mmol/L and LDH 1800 U/L, but cultures are negative. He is treated for empyema with a chest drain and antibiotics. Two weeks later he re-presents with a right-sided pleural effusion, pleuritic pain, fever and a symmetrical small-joint polyarthritis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
set.explanation: The film shows a large left pleural effusion. Rheumatoid effusions are exudates with very low glucose (often below 1.6 mmol/L), low pH and high LDH, so they mimic empyema; they are commoner in men and can precede or accompany the arthritis, and a new contralateral effusion with symmetrical polyarthritis reveals the diagnosis (check rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP). Recurrent empyema on the other side would be unusual, and lung cancer, lymphoma and mesothelioma do not cause inflammatory polyarthritis with this fluid profile.

Sinusitis, conductive deafness (otitis media), stridor from subglottic stenosis and multiple bilateral lung nodules with constitutional symptoms are the ear, nose and airway plus lung pattern of granulomatosis with polyangiitis; c-ANCA (PR3), urinalysis for nephritis and biopsy confirm it. EGPA needs asthma and eosinophilia, eosinophilic pneumonias cause infiltrates rather than nodules and do not involve the ear or subglottis, and multiple nodules in a non-smoker with ENT disease are unlikely to be a bronchial carcinoma.

Chronic beryllium disease is a beryllium-specific T-cell granulomatous disorder that is clinically and histologically indistinguishable from sarcoidosis (bilateral hilar nodes, non-caseating granulomas); occupational exposure is the clue, and a positive beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test confirms it. Sarcoidosis should be diagnosed only after beryllium exposure is excluded. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis from damp does not cause hilar lymphadenopathy, silicosis causes upper-zone nodules with eggshell nodal calcification, and dysfunctional breathing gives a normal X-ray.

Diffuse ground-glass opacity with poorly defined centrilobular nodules is the typical HRCT pattern of non-fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis, and a pet parrot provides the avian antigen (bird fancier's lung); avian precipitins and bronchoalveolar lavage lymphocytosis support the diagnosis, and antigen avoidance is the key treatment. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis shows basal subpleural reticulation and honeycombing, sarcoidosis shows perilymphatic nodules and hilar nodes, a breathing artefact does not produce nodules, and aspirin sensitivity causes asthma and nasal polyps.

Francisella tularensis is carried by rabbits, hares and muskrats and by ticks, and tularaemia can present as pneumonia after handling infected animals. The other pairs are wrong: anthrax is linked to hides and wool (unpasteurised milk transmits Brucella and Coxiella), Chlamydia psittaci comes from birds, Coxiella burnetii (Q fever) from sheep, cattle and goats especially at birth, and leptospirosis from rat urine in sewers or fresh water rather than welding.

set.stem: A 78-year-old woman has multilobar pneumonia requiring intubation. Arterial blood gas on a high inspired oxygen concentration shows PaO2 7.2 kPa (54 mmHg). What is the main cause of the hypoxaemia?
set.explanation: Alveoli filled with exudate are perfused but not ventilated, so blood passes through them without gas exchange, a true right-to-left shunt; the hallmark is hypoxaemia that barely improves with high inspired oxygen. V/Q mismatch (low but non-zero ventilation) corrects readily with supplemental oxygen, hypoventilation is excluded because she is mechanically ventilated and it would raise the PaCO2, and diffusion limitation is not the problem. PEEP to recruit flooded alveoli is the key ventilator strategy.

set.stem: A 38-year-old woman who recently started smoking develops a 5-day febrile illness with rapidly progressive respiratory failure and diffuse bilateral infiltrates. Bronchoalveolar lavage shows 40% eosinophils, blood cultures and respiratory viral PCR are negative, and she has been on broad-spectrum antibiotics for 48 hours without improvement. What is the best treatment now?
set.explanation: Acute eosinophilic pneumonia, often triggered by new smoking or vaping, causes acute febrile hypoxaemic respiratory failure with more than 25% eosinophils in lavage fluid (peripheral eosinophilia may be absent initially); it responds dramatically to high-dose corticosteroids such as IV methylprednisolone, and relapse is rare. Surgical biopsy is unnecessary once lavage is diagnostic, continuing antibiotics alone ignores the diagnosis, and oseltamivir and co-trimoxazole treat influenza and Pneumocystis, which cultures and the clinical picture do not support.

why: Same idea as resinf-0009 (chronic purulent sputum: HRCT confirms bronchiectasis)

set.stem: A 62-year-old woman has focal bronchiectasis after Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) infection, which has been treated. Her sputum cultures are now negative but she still produces sputum every day. What is the best treatment?
set.explanation: Daily airway clearance, taught by a respiratory physiotherapist (active cycle of breathing, oscillating positive expiratory pressure devices such as a flutter valve, postural drainage), is recommended by BTS guidance for every patient with bronchiectasis and chronic sputum. Lobectomy is reserved for localised disease with uncontrolled symptoms or bleeding despite medical therapy, the MAC regimen is not continued once cultures convert and the course is complete, dornase alfa helps in cystic fibrosis but may be harmful in non-CF bronchiectasis, and prednisone has no role.

set.stem: Which finding is expected on bronchoalveolar lavage in diffuse alveolar haemorrhage?
set.explanation: In diffuse alveolar haemorrhage, sequential lavage aliquots become progressively bloodier and alveolar macrophages ingest red cells, becoming haemosiderin-laden (Prussian blue-positive) within 48–72 hours. Causes include ANCA vasculitis, anti-GBM disease and SLE. Milky fluid with foamy macrophages indicates alveolar proteinosis, ferruginous bodies asbestos exposure, a raised CD4:CD8 lymphocytosis sarcoidosis, and atypical type II pneumocytes drug toxicity or diffuse alveolar damage.

set.stem: A 56-year-old man has subacute fever, cough and breathlessness with patchy alveolar infiltrates that do not respond to antibiotics. Lung biopsy shows plugs of granulation tissue filling the distal airways and alveolar ducts (organising pneumonia pattern). What is the best therapy?
set.explanation: Cryptogenic organising pneumonia typically follows a flu-like illness with migratory consolidation unresponsive to antibiotics, and responds rapidly to oral corticosteroids (prednisolone about 0.75–1 mg/kg tapered over 6–12 months); relapse on tapering is common but usually steroid-responsive. Nintedanib and pirfenidone are antifibrotics for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, azathioprine is only a steroid-sparing option, and transplantation is not needed for a steroid-responsive condition.

set.stem: A 52-year-old woman has progressive breathlessness; CT shows extensive calcified mediastinal soft tissue encasing and narrowing the central airways and pulmonary vessels (fibrosing mediastinitis). Which statement is true?
set.explanation: Fibrosing mediastinitis is an excessive fibrotic response to previous granulomatous infection, most often Histoplasma capsulatum in endemic areas and tuberculosis elsewhere. The infection is burnt out, so antigen tests are usually negative and antifungal drugs and steroids do not reverse the fibrosis; surgery is hazardous, and symptomatic stenoses are managed with endovascular or airway stenting.

set.stem: A 35-year-old farmer develops cough, wheeze, breathlessness and fever a few hours after working in a barn with stored hay. He has smoked 10 cigarettes a day for 6 months and runs marathons. His grandfather had asthma as a child, and he has lived in central London for the past year. What is the most likely cause of his condition?
set.explanation: Symptoms starting 4–8 hours after exposure to mouldy hay are acute hypersensitivity pneumonitis (farmer's lung), caused by inhaled thermophilic actinomycetes such as Saccharopolyspora rectivirgula, so his occupation is the cause; avoidance or respiratory protection prevents progression to fibrosis. Six months of smoking cannot cause COPD, a grandfather with childhood asthma adds little risk, exercise-induced symptoms occur during or just after exercise, and air pollution would not explain the timing after barn work.

Streptococcus pneumoniae is the commonest cause of community-acquired pneumonia at all ages, accounting for roughly a third to a half of cases in which a pathogen is identified. Haemophilus influenzae is important in COPD, Legionella causes outbreaks linked to water systems, Staphylococcus aureus follows influenza, and Aspergillus causes lung disease mainly in asthmatics or the immunocompromised. Empirical antibiotics therefore always cover pneumococcus.

CURB-65 scores one point each for new Confusion, Urea above 7 mmol/L, Respiratory rate of 30/min or more, low Blood pressure (systolic below 90 or diastolic 60 mmHg or less) and age 65 or over. A respiratory rate of 20/min is below the threshold and is not a criterion. Scores of 0–1 are low severity (home treatment), 2 moderate (hospital), and 3–5 high severity (consider critical care).

Mycoplasma pneumoniae causes an atypical pneumonia with prominent extrapulmonary features: erythema multiforme (target lesions on the hands), cold-agglutinin (IgM) autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, myringitis, hepatitis, myocarditis and Guillain–Barré syndrome. It occurs in epidemics every few years and is treated with a macrolide or doxycycline, since it has no cell wall and is resistant to beta-lactams. Chlamydia pneumoniae, Haemophilus, Staphylococcus and Legionella do not cause this combination.

Chlamydia psittaci is acquired by inhaling dried droppings or secretions from infected birds, especially parrots and budgerigars, and causes psittacosis: a flu-like illness with headache, myalgia, dry cough and sometimes splenomegaly, relative bradycardia or rash. Treatment is doxycycline (a macrolide as an alternative). The other organisms have no link with bird exposure.

Injecting drug users are at high risk of Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia from skin flora introduced at injection sites, and lung infection may be haematogenous (septic emboli from tricuspid endocarditis) or community-acquired, often cavitating with abscesses and empyema. Blood cultures and echocardiography are essential, and antibiotics must cover S. aureus including MRSA where prevalent. The other organisms cause pneumonia but have no particular association with injecting drug use.
